How we pick the best Apple deals

John Ternus could be forgiven for having second thoughts about this whole CEO thing. It all seemed so simple a few months ago: a typically unselfish Tim Cook had saved up multiple groundbreaking products so his successor could unveil them in the first few months of his tenure and hit the ground running. But it turns out that innovation is a double-edged sword, not an easy win.

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first ever folding phone, should have been a celebration of the company’s best qualities. A classic example of Apple’s patient perfectionism, the device was as thoughtfully designed as it was late to market. Arriving just as foldables threatened to break into the mainstream (it will accelerate this process by its very existence, of course), the Duo corrected many common issues: its stubbier form factor means the internal screen is rectangular, not square; the clever hinge design looks superb and feels reassuringly robust; and that matte-finish inner screen delivers one of the least obtrusive creases on the market right now.

But then disaster struck. A number of units proved seriously defective, failing to open or close properly, making strange noises, or displaying unwanted lines on the screen. So much for that robust hinge. It was probably a bad batch rather than a fundamental issue with the design, but enough customers were affected for Apple to be moved to make a public statement and publish a troubleshooting guide. And then, to add insult to injury, some affected users (who’d each paid out at least $1,999) had to wait for replacements because of supply shortages.

Of course, the Duo’s problems can’t entirely be blamed on its innovative design. The 18 Pro, which was launched at the same time, offers largely the same design and feature set as its predecessor but suffered issues of its own, including crackling speakers, random reboots, and an inability to place emergency calls. But in most cases these were bugs which could be quickly fixed via software, not device-breaking faults. They certainly garnered less media coverage than Hingegate, and most observers would regard the 18 Pro as more of a success than the Duo, at least in the short term.

The Duo, then, was not the straightforward slam dunk John Ternus must have hoped for, nor did it start his reign with an easy win. It was a complicated and problematic launch: interesting, risky, flawed. Apple, however, kept on going. October brought the announcement of two more groundbreaking Apple launches in the form of its first ever touchscreen laptop and its first smart home hub. However, neither proved to be the simple success which any newbie CEO longs for.

Most reviewers, I will grant you, love the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. (My colleague Roman Loyola says it “raises the bar of Apple excellence.”) But the positive notes have a curious equivocation about the marquee feature. The display is amazing, but why did Apple feel the give it a touchscreen, with all of the corresponding price and design compromises? “It’s not a spotlight feature,” says Roman. “Touch isn’t even in the name of this new MacBook. I’d go so far as to say that the laptop just happens to have Touch. Apple hasn’t done anything here that requires Touch, so you can buy it, never use Touch, and you won’t miss out on anything.”

So, the single thing that’s truly new is almost tangential to the laptop’s usefulness. Which even in a five-star review must be an oddly disappointing response to one of Apple’s most radical Mac launches in years.

Still, it could have been a lot worse, and in fact, it soon would be. The HomeView home hub is yet another entirely new venture for the company, which means both excitement and risk. And the risk part of the equation came to the forefront as hundreds of buyers complained about dozens of separate software issues with their brand-new devices. One commenter called it the “worst Apple launch ever” (do the words “hockey-puck mouse” mean nothing to you?) and the atmosphere could only be described as mutinous.

My suspicion, after conferring with another colleague who’s been testing out a unit and then asking Apple’s product managers for their thoughts, is that HomeView will turn out to be more 18 Pro than Duo. Even the “worst launch ever” commenter conceded that the HomeView’s hardware is strong; it just has lots of bugs. Or perhaps I should say had lots of bugs, because that same colleague found that updating the device’s software delivered a much smoother experience than was reported elsewhere, and Apple has since mobilized to roll out further patches. Not everything will work perfectly, as is always the case with new products, but software tends to be a lot easier to fix than hardware.

So it’s been a mixed bag of a tenure so far for John Ternus. He’s had the privilege of unveiling three of the most momentous Apple products of the decade, and the burden of responding to those products’ inevitable teething troubles.

First, novelty means unfamiliarity: I’ve been using the iPhone Duo for several weeks and still find the physical design awkward and the software interface confusing. It will take time to get used to both of those factors, just as it will take time to grow accustomed to using touch on a laptop, or to find space in our lives for a home hub with a screen. It’s easier to understand the purpose of a product if you’ve already used one that’s essentially the same.

Second, entirely new products are difficult to develop because so much needs to be designed from scratch. The iPhone Duo’s hinge is a miracle of modern engineering, but that doesn’t make it immune to manufacturing errors; rather, because it’s so new and so innovative, they become almost inevitable. The HomeView software platform is also completely new, which means more to test and more scope to miss bugs. The tech industry worships the new, but new things break. It’s part of the deal.

There have been ups and downs, but I’ve enjoyed Apple’s bold new approach this fall. With the Duo, the company dared to try something new after umpteen near-identical iPhone updates; with the touchscreen MacBook and HomeView it showed a willingness to radically evolve a successful existing product and to move into an entirely new market. The company took risks, and was punished as much as it was rewarded.

Looking at this fall’s complaints and controversies, it’s easy to see why massive corporations are tempted to play it safe most of the time. And why, in the past, Apple has so often favored cautious iteration. Releasing a mildly tweaked version of a product which was already successful is, ironically, exactly the sort of easy win which John Ternus must have craved. Actual innovation is a nightmare that goes wrong as often as it goes right. And when it fails, an innovative product fails in public.

But as risky and occasionally embarrassing as it can be, innovation is still the way forward. I’m sure that in time Apple’s turn towards radical innovation this year will prove to be not just the correct but the necessary decision. You can’t make the same product forever. It just might have been kinder to take at least some of the risks before the new guy took over.

Should you buy a Mac or MacBook now or wait for a better deal?

With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need a Mac immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if it matches or approaches a previous low for the same configuration. Waiting can be a gamble if you’re buying clearance stock with a particular screen size, memory capacity, or finish. If the retailer discount is close to Apple’s gift card value and you already have another Apple purchase planned, it may be worth waiting until November 27 to take advantage of Apple’s gift card offer, but note that MacBook Neo, standard M6 MacBook Pro, iMac and Mac Studio are not included in Apple’s Black Friday deal.

The M5 MacBook Air remains an appealing purchase at a good discount, with a replacement not expected until 2027. The recently updated Mac mini and Mac Studio are also worth considering if they meet your needs. The main reason to wait is a better price rather than an imminent replacement.

MacBook Pro buyers no longer need to wait for the rumored October launches: the standard M6 and OLED touchscreen models are now available. However, their recent arrival may limit initial discounts. Non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max models could offer better value, particularly if you don’t need the touchscreen version’s improved display and lighter design. If your existing M4 or M5 MacBook Pro still meets your needs, there’s little reason to upgrade simply because a newer option exists.

The M6 iMac has only just arrived, replacing the aging M4 version. Compare a modest saving on the latest model with a substantial clearance discount on its predecessor, rather than assuming the older machine is automatically the better deal.

Previous prices need context this year. Following June’s increases, a discount from Apple’s current asking price may still leave you paying more than before the increases. Compare retailers as well: Amazon competes with Best Buy, Walmart, and B&H in the U.S., and retailers including Currys and John Lewis in the U.K. Our MacBook Pro buying advice explains the current choices.

Which Mac specifications are worth paying for?

The cheapest Mac isn’t always the best value. Use Black Friday to get a configuration that will serve you for longer within your budget, but don’t pay for performance or features you won’t use.

Check the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. A standard M6 and an M5 Pro or M5 Max serve different needs: the newer generation number alone doesn’t tell you which is better for your work. For MacBook Pro listings, distinguish the OLED touchscreen version from non-touch models.

Avoid saving a small amount by buying too little memory or storage. Most current Macs start with 16GB of unified memory, but the MacBook Neo has a fixed 8GB, and some desktop configurations include only a 256GB SSD. Unified memory cannot be upgraded later. An external SSD can add storage, but it cannot compensate for insufficient RAM.

Once the processor meets your needs, additional memory may be more useful than a faster chip. Compare a discounted Air with the Neo, too: the M5 Air starts with twice the memory and storage of the entry-level Neo. Our Mac buying guide explains which specifications suit different workloads.

Check whether the configuration includes nano-texture glass. This optional finish reduces glare and reflections, which can help in bright rooms or near windows, but increases the price. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may offer better value.

Should you buy an older Mac or MacBook?

Foundry

An older Mac can be excellent value if its price reflects its age and configuration. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of the newer equivalent, rather than focusing on a large percentage saving from its original launch price.

Previous-generation Apple silicon models are the most promising starting point. A discounted M4 MacBook Air or standard M5 MacBook Pro may meet your needs comfortably. Older Pro and Max configurations can also be worth considering if they provide the memory, graphics performance, and connections your work requires for substantially less money.

Check what the saving buys—and what you give up. An older Mac with more memory or storage could be more useful than a newer entry-level configuration. Conversely, a cheaper older Air with 256GB storage isn’t directly comparable with an M5 Air that starts with 512GB. The non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros also remain current options, despite the arrival of the standard M6 and touchscreen models.

Be much more cautious with Intel Macs. Their software support is winding down, and a low purchase price may leave you with a machine that has a limited useful life for current apps and macOS features. Check compatibility with the software you need before buying any older model.

For used or refurbished Macs, check battery condition on laptops, warranty coverage, and the returns policy. Confirm that Activation Lock has been removed and that the Mac isn’t still enrolled in an organization’s management system.

Mac or MacBook deals to avoid

Treat large advertised discounts carefully. Following June’s price increases, “$400 off” may simply bring a Mac closer to what it cost before the increase. Compare previous selling prices for the same configuration, rather than judging the offer solely against today’s recommended price.

Check whether the price includes AppleCare+ or another protection plan. Some Amazon listings bundle coverage with the Mac. If you don’t want it, a listing without coverage could be cheaper; if you do, compare the bundle with buying the Mac and coverage separately.

Check for a bundled power adapter, too. Some Mac laptops are sold without one in the U.K. and EU. A charger bundle may be useful if you need an adapter, but could mean paying extra unnecessarily if you already own a suitable one.

Compare the complete setup cost. A Mac mini or Studio requires a display, keyboard, and mouse or trackpad, while adapters and docks can add to the cost of any Mac.

Finally, distinguish cash discounts from gift cards, trade-ins, financing, and membership-only offers. Read the conditions, check the seller, and confirm whether the Mac is new, refurbished, or used, along with its warranty and returns policy.

How we choose Mac and MacBook deals

Macworld has covered the Mac since its launch in 1984, and our recommendations draw on decades of experience and hands-on reviews. We consider performance, display quality, battery life, portability, connectivity, and everyday use alongside price to explain which Macs suit different buyers.

Our reviews help us assess which upgrades are worth paying for. We look at whether additional processing power benefits demanding workloads, when more memory is useful, and whether a premium display justifies the extra cost. A MacBook Air may offer better value for everyday work, while a Pro, Max, or Ultra configuration needs to earn its higher price through the work it enables.

We combine those findings with current prices and previous offers, matching the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. Following Apple’s June price increases, we also consider earlier selling prices rather than judging a deal solely against today’s recommended retail price. A large advertised discount doesn’t automatically make an offer exceptional.

We consider the complete purchase, too: the retailer, product condition, warranty, and any conditions attached to the price. Should you buy a Mac or MacBook now or wait for a better deal?

With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need a Mac immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if it matches or approaches a previous low for the same configuration. Waiting can be a gamble if you’re buying clearance stock with a particular screen size, memory capacity, or finish. If the retailer discount is close to Apple’s gift card value and you already have another Apple purchase planned, it may be worth waiting until November 27 to take advantage of Apple’s gift card offer, but note that MacBook Neo, standard M6 MacBook Pro, iMac and Mac Studio are not included in Apple’s Black Friday deal.

The M5 MacBook Air remains an appealing purchase at a good discount, with a replacement not expected until 2027. The recently updated Mac mini and Mac Studio are also worth considering if they meet your needs. The main reason to wait is a better price rather than an imminent replacement.

MacBook Pro buyers no longer need to wait for the rumored October launches: the standard M6 and OLED touchscreen models are now available. However, their recent arrival may limit initial discounts. Non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max models could offer better value, particularly if you don’t need the touchscreen version’s improved display and lighter design. If your existing M4 or M5 MacBook Pro still meets your needs, there’s little reason to upgrade simply because a newer option exists.

The M6 iMac has only just arrived, replacing the aging M4 version. Compare a modest saving on the latest model with a substantial clearance discount on its predecessor, rather than assuming the older machine is automatically the better deal.

Previous prices need context this year. Following June’s increases, a discount from Apple’s current asking price may still leave you paying more than before the increases. Compare retailers as well: Amazon competes with Best Buy, Walmart, and B&H in the U.S., and retailers including Currys and John Lewis in the U.K. Our MacBook Pro buying advice explains the current choices.

Which Mac specifications are worth paying for?

The cheapest Mac isn’t always the best value. Use Black Friday to get a configuration that will serve you for longer within your budget, but don’t pay for performance or features you won’t use.

Check the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. A standard M6 and an M5 Pro or M5 Max serve different needs: the newer generation number alone doesn’t tell you which is better for your work. For MacBook Pro listings, distinguish the OLED touchscreen version from non-touch models.

Avoid saving a small amount by buying too little memory or storage. Most current Macs start with 16GB of unified memory, but the MacBook Neo has a fixed 8GB, and some desktop configurations include only a 256GB SSD. Unified memory cannot be upgraded later. An external SSD can add storage, but it cannot compensate for insufficient RAM.

Once the processor meets your needs, additional memory may be more useful than a faster chip. Compare a discounted Air with the Neo, too: the M5 Air starts with twice the memory and storage of the entry-level Neo. Our Mac buying guide explains which specifications suit different workloads.

Check whether the configuration includes nano-texture glass. This optional finish reduces glare and reflections, which can help in bright rooms or near windows, but increases the price. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may offer better value.

Should you buy an older Mac or MacBook?

Foundry

An older Mac can be excellent value if its price reflects its age and configuration. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of the newer equivalent, rather than focusing on a large percentage saving from its original launch price.

Previous-generation Apple silicon models are the most promising starting point. A discounted M4 MacBook Air or standard M5 MacBook Pro may meet your needs comfortably. Older Pro and Max configurations can also be worth considering if they provide the memory, graphics performance, and connections your work requires for substantially less money.

Check what the saving buys—and what you give up. An older Mac with more memory or storage could be more useful than a newer entry-level configuration. Conversely, a cheaper older Air with 256GB storage isn’t directly comparable with an M5 Air that starts with 512GB. The non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros also remain current options, despite the arrival of the standard M6 and touchscreen models.

Be much more cautious with Intel Macs. Their software support is winding down, and a low purchase price may leave you with a machine that has a limited useful life for current apps and macOS features. Check compatibility with the software you need before buying any older model.

For used or refurbished Macs, check battery condition on laptops, warranty coverage, and the returns policy. Confirm that Activation Lock has been removed and that the Mac isn’t still enrolled in an organization’s management system.

Mac or MacBook deals to avoid

Treat large advertised discounts carefully. Following June’s price increases, “$400 off” may simply bring a Mac closer to what it cost before the increase. Compare previous selling prices for the same configuration, rather than judging the offer solely against today’s recommended price.

Check whether the price includes AppleCare+ or another protection plan. Some Amazon listings bundle coverage with the Mac. If you don’t want it, a listing without coverage could be cheaper; if you do, compare the bundle with buying the Mac and coverage separately.

Check for a bundled power adapter, too. Some Mac laptops are sold without one in the U.K. and EU. A charger bundle may be useful if you need an adapter, but could mean paying extra unnecessarily if you already own a suitable one.

Compare the complete setup cost. A Mac mini or Studio requires a display, keyboard, and mouse or trackpad, while adapters and docks can add to the cost of any Mac.

Finally, distinguish cash discounts from gift cards, trade-ins, financing, and membership-only offers. Read the conditions, check the seller, and confirm whether the Mac is new, refurbished, or used, along with its warranty and returns policy.

How we choose Mac and MacBook deals

Macworld has covered the Mac since its launch in 1984, and our recommendations draw on decades of experience and hands-on reviews. We consider performance, display quality, battery life, portability, connectivity, and everyday use alongside price to explain which Macs suit different buyers.

Our reviews help us assess which upgrades are worth paying for. We look at whether additional processing power benefits demanding workloads, when more memory is useful, and whether a premium display justifies the extra cost. A MacBook Air may offer better value for everyday work, while a Pro, Max, or Ultra configuration needs to earn its higher price through the work it enables.

We combine those findings with current prices and previous offers, matching the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. Following Apple’s June price increases, we also consider earlier selling prices rather than judging a deal solely against today’s recommended retail price. A large advertised discount doesn’t automatically make an offer exceptional.

We consider the complete purchase, too: the retailer, product condition, warranty, and any conditions attached to the price. For desktop Macs, we also account for the display and accessories you’ll need. Our Mac buying guide and MacBook comparison explain how to choose the right model and configuration.

USB-C and its Thunderbolt variant are the most up-to-date standards of the USB connector. They allow data-transfer speeds of up to 80Gbps, can fast-charge devices up to 240W, and conveniently fit in a port either way up—which means that you can wave bye-bye to the age-old USB guessing game of “Which way does it go in?”.

USB-C is no one-trick pony—handling data transfer, video output and power input. You’ll find faster variants of USB-C (called Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5) on Macs. Each version of Thunderbolt is backwards compatible with USB-C so the adapters reviewed here will all work with modern Macs—from the MacBooks Neo, Air and Pro, through to the desktop iMac, Mac mini and Studio. USB-C’s 5-10Gbps speeds will limit some of Thunderbolt’s more impressive 40 to 80Gbps potential but for most people even 5Gbps is fast enough. If super-fast data transfer is one of your requirements, a number of hubs reviewed below do use Thunderbolt or 40Gbps USB4. Find out more in our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 comparison and also our chart at the end showing all the ports of Apple’s recent Macs.

Apple

In general, an “adapter” works with a single port (such as USB-A or Ethernet) while a “hub” gives you multiple ports. If you require even more, then look for a “docking station” or “dock“. Docks usually come with their own power supply, while hubs require a separate USB-C charger if you need a power source. If you’re after a full desktop setup for your MacBook, look out for our recommendations for the best USB-C and Thunderbolt docking stations for MacBooks.

Apple sells its own range of USB-C adapters to HDMI, VGA and more, but they are overpriced and underpowered compared to the premium USB-C hubs and adapters we have reviewed here. We haven’t included the many much cheaper but lower-quality versions you can find online as we recommend only from trusted and tested makers. There are plenty of affordable solutions tested and reviewed here that are of a higher quality.

Look for each hub’s video capability for connecting to external displays. Most support only one monitor, but some offer two—note that more than two usually requires an extra software install.

Passthrough power will likely also be of interest to MacBook users. 60W Power Delivery (PD) will work even for the 16-inch MacBook Pro (just), but more watts equals a faster charge.

Note that the ports on the MacBook Neo are USB-C and only one of them is properly data-ready at 10Gbps, with the other just for charging. Read more on how the MacBook Neo’s USB-C ports are different. As it has just one data port, a USB-C hub becomes a must for expanding the Neo’s potential—read our roundup of the best MacBook Neo accessories.

Which extra ports do you need in a hub

Many MacBook users connect their laptop to one or more external displays for greater screen space. You can connect to monitors using USB-C (via adapters to non-USB-C monitors) or better a dedicated video port, such as HDMI or DisplayPort. Check the hub specs to see which displays they support: some are limited to HD displays, others support 4K (also known as UHD) displays. The refresh rate is also important. 4K at 30Hz is fine for most productivity and browsing tasks, but watching video or playing games demands higher refresh rates of at least 60Hz.

You may need some legacy non-reversible USB-A ports, and most adapters and hubs have at least one for your non-USB-C memory sticks and drives. Look for at least USB 3.0, which has a speedy bandwidth of 5Gbps compared to the lamentably sluggish USB 2.0’s 480Mbps.

To fast-charge an iPhone, you need a minimum of 18W and it has to be USB-C, so look for extra USB-C slots with charging power, which are more capable than USB-A.

Other ports to look for in a hub include Ethernet for faster wired Internet access (without the flakiness of Wi-Fi). You can choose from standard Gigabit Ethernet (1000Mbps) or 2.5Gb and even 5Gb and 10Gb Ethernet (2500-10000Mbps), although the faster Ethernet requires the whole network to support that speed.

An SD or microSD card reader is perfect for adding inexpensive portable storage to your system. Card readers come at different speeds: UHS-I at 104MBps, and UHS-II at 312MBps; although some are slower at 60MBps.

Look for hubs that offer passthrough charging, so you can charge your laptop even though you are using up one of the laptop’s USB-C ports for the hub itself. Most don’t ship with a charger, so you’ll need to add your own, and remember that it needs to be a 100W charger to give 85W and above charging if offered by the hub. Lower wattage chargers are fine but will limit the hub’s charging potential. Couple your hub with one of the best Mac USB-C chargers. See how much power your MacBook needs in our advice below the list of recommended hubs and adapters.

You can also buy USB-C adapters for the many older display standards out there, such as VGA and DVI. We’ve picked the best for you below.

Many hubs and docks aren’t compatible with Apple’s SuperDrive CD/DVD drive. We’ve found few dock makers that offers compatibility with the SuperDrive, the Caldigit Thunderbolt Element Hub and OWC Thunderbolt Dock being two that do.

Here are the onboard ports on all of Apple’s current and recent Macs:

Mirrored or Extended Modes for Mac displays

When you attach more than one external display to a Mac you can choose between various setups. Most hubs with more than one video port—usually HDMI—can mirror your MacBook’s screen, but most can at best handle showing a different screen to the Mac but not different to each other when attempting Extended Mode.

For full extended Mode, where each of the screens shows a different image and you treat each as an extension to your workspace—moving your cursor and windows easily between the displays—you will likely need a hub or dock that supports free third-party DisplayLink software, which is easy to download and install. Included above are reviews of the Plugable Dual and Quad HDMI adapters, both of which work with DisplayLink. DisplayLink enables multiple screens even with plain M1 and M2 MacBooks that are technically limited to just one external display.

How much power does each MacBook require for smooth running

Check the Power Delivery (PD) charging power each hub or adapter offers connected laptops or iPads.

  • The MacBook Neo charges at 20W.
  • The 13-inch MacBook Air charges at 30W, but can fast-charge at 70W and above.
  • The 13-inch MacBook Pro and 15-inch MacBook Air charge at 70W for fast charging, but even 45W would keep you topped up if running basic tasks at the time. Apple recommends at least 60W for the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro.
  • The higher-end 14-inch (M3/M4/M5/M6, M4/M5 Pro/Max) and 16-inch MacBook Pro require at least 96W for fast charging, but can cope at 60W or 70W. The 16-inch MacBook Pro prefers 140W, but is fine with 94W unless under extreme processing tasks.

You can certainly use a charger at lower power, but remember that it will power up slower than when using a higher-wattage charger, and if too low your laptop might run out of juice altogether when maxed out on power-hungry apps and devices. And you can use a higher-power charger without any concerns. The device being charged decides how much power it requires.

USB-C and its Thunderbolt variant are the most up-to-date standards of the USB connector. They allow data-transfer speeds of up to 80Gbps, can fast-charge devices up to 240W, and conveniently fit in a port either way up—which means that you can wave bye-bye to the age-old USB guessing game of “Which way does it go in?”.

USB-C is no one-trick pony—handling data transfer, video output and power input. You’ll find faster variants of USB-C (called Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5) on Macs. Each version of Thunderbolt is backwards compatible with USB-C so the adapters reviewed here will all work with modern Macs—from the MacBooks Neo, Air and Pro, through to the desktop iMac, Mac mini and Studio. USB-C’s 5-10Gbps speeds will limit some of Thunderbolt’s more impressive 40 to 80Gbps potential but for most people even 5Gbps is fast enough. If super-fast data transfer is one of your requirements, a number of hubs reviewed below do use Thunderbolt or 40Gbps USB4. Find out more in our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 comparison and also our chart at the end showing all the ports of Apple’s recent Macs.

In general, an “adapter” works with a single port (such as USB-A or Ethernet) while a “hub” gives you multiple ports. If you require even more, then look for a “docking station” or “dock“. Docks usually come with their own power supply, while hubs require a separate USB-C charger if you need a power source. If you’re after a full desktop setup for your MacBook, look out for our recommendations for the best USB-C and Thunderbolt docking stations for MacBooks.

Which extra ports do you need in a hub

Many MacBook users connect their laptop to one or more external displays for greater screen space. You can connect to monitors using USB-C (via adapters to non-USB-C monitors) or better a dedicated video port, such as HDMI or DisplayPort. Check the hub specs to see which displays they support: some are limited to HD displays, others support 4K (also known as UHD) displays. The refresh rate is also important. 4K at 30Hz is fine for most productivity and browsing tasks, but watching video or playing games demands higher refresh rates of at least 60Hz.

You may need some legacy non-reversible USB-A ports, and most adapters and hubs have at least one for your non-USB-C memory sticks and drives. Look for at least USB 3.0, which has a speedy bandwidth of 5Gbps compared to the lamentably sluggish USB 2.0’s 480Mbps.

To fast-charge an iPhone, you need a minimum of 18W and it has to be USB-C, so look for extra USB-C slots with charging power, which are more capable than USB-A.

Other ports to look for in a hub include Ethernet for faster wired Internet access (without the flakiness of Wi-Fi). You can choose from standard Gigabit Ethernet (1000Mbps) or 2.5Gb and even 5Gb and 10Gb Ethernet (2500-10000Mbps), although the faster Ethernet requires the whole network to support that speed.

An SD or microSD card reader is perfect for adding inexpensive portable storage to your system. Card readers come at different speeds: UHS-I at 104MBps, and UHS-II at 312MBps; although some are slower at 60MBps.

Look for hubs that offer passthrough charging, so you can charge your laptop even though you are using up one of the laptop’s USB-C ports for the hub itself. Most don’t ship with a charger, so you’ll need to add your own, and remember that it needs to be a 100W charger to give 85W and above charging if offered by the hub. Lower wattage chargers are fine but will limit the hub’s charging potential. Couple your hub with one of the best Mac USB-C chargers. See how much power your MacBook needs in our advice below the list of recommended hubs and adapters.

You can also buy USB-C adapters for the many older display standards out there, such as VGA and DVI. We’ve picked the best for you below.

Many hubs and docks aren’t compatible with Apple’s SuperDrive CD/DVD drive. We’ve found few dock makers that offers compatibility with the SuperDrive, the Caldigit Thunderbolt Element Hub and OWC Thunderbolt Dock being two that do.

  • MacBook Neo: 2x USB-C (one for 10Gbps data and one for charging), 3.5mm headphone jack
  • MacBook Air: 2x Thunderbolt 4, MagSafe 3 charging port, 3.5mm headphone jack
  • MacBook Pro (plain M4/M5/M6): 3x Thunderbolt 4, MagSafe 3 charging port, HDMI, SDXC Card Reader (250MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
  • MacBook Pro (M4/M5 Pro/Max): 3x Thunderbolt 5, MagSafe 3 charging port, HDMI, SDXC Card Reader (250MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
  • iMac (24-inch): 2x Thunderbolt 4/USB4 or 4x Thunderbolt 4, 3.5mm headphone jack, optional Gigabit Ethernet
  • Mac mini M4/M6: 3x Thunderbolt 4, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), HDMI, Gigabit Ethernet, 3.5mm headphone jack

Mirrored or Extended Modes for Mac displays

When you attach more than one external display to a Mac you can choose between various setups. Most hubs with more than one video port—usually HDMI—can mirror your MacBook’s screen, but most can at best handle showing a different screen to the Mac but not different to each other when attempting Extended Mode.

For full extended Mode, where each of the screens shows a different image and you treat each as an extension to your workspace—moving your cursor and windows easily between the displays—you will likely need a hub or dock that supports free third-party DisplayLink software, which is easy to download and install. Included above are reviews of the Plugable Dual and Quad HDMI adapters, both of which work with DisplayLink. DisplayLink enables multiple screens even with plain M1 and M2 MacBooks that are technically limited to just one external display.

If you need even more ports than you’ll find on a hub, check our reviews of the best DisplayLink docks.

How much power does each MacBook require for smooth running

Check the Power Delivery (PD) charging power each hub or adapter offers connected laptops or iPads.

  • The MacBook Neo charges at 20W.
  • The 13-inch MacBook Air charges at 30W, but can fast-charge at 70W and above.
  • The 13-inch MacBook Pro and 15-inch MacBook Air charge at 70W for fast charging, but even 45W would keep you topped up if running basic tasks at the time. Apple recommends at least 60W for the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro.
  • The higher-end 14-inch (M3/M4/M5/M6, M4/M5 Pro/Max) and 16-inch MacBook Pro require at least 96W for fast charging, but can cope at 60W or 70W. The 16-inch MacBook Pro prefers 140W, but is fine with 94W unless under extreme processing tasks.

You can certainly use a charger at lower power, but remember that it will power up slower than when using a higher-wattage charger, and if too low your laptop might run out of juice altogether when maxed out on power-hungry apps and devices. And you can use a higher-power charger without any concerns. The device being charged decides how much power it requires.

Does Apple have sales?

Apple rarely discounts its own products. Even during its annual Black Friday shopping event, which runs from Black Friday to Cyber Monday, Apple typically offers gift cards with eligible purchases instead of cutting prices.

That doesn’t mean you have to pay full price. Third-party retailers such as Amazon, Best Buy and other Apple resellers regularly discount Apple products throughout the year.

Some of the best savings on Apple products come during Amazon’s Prime Day events. We saw substantial discounts during the Prime Days in June 2026 and in October 2026.

Apple also offers year-round education discounts to students, teachers and education staff. During its annual Back To School promotion – usually running for around three months from June or July in many countries (and from January in Australia, New Zealand and other Southern Hemisphere markets) – eligible higher education students can receive a free pair of AirPods or an Apple Pencil with selected Mac and iPad purchases.

Finally, don’t overlook the Apple Certified Refurbished Store, where you can buy refurbished Macs, iPads and other Apple products at a discount. These devices are thoroughly tested, include a new battery and outer casing where applicable, and come with the same one-year warranty as new Apple products. Following Apple’s June 2026 price increases, some refurbished models can be particularly attractive because their prices haven’t risen in the same way as equivalent new models.

FAQ

1.

When are the best Apple deals?

Apple deals are generally best during major retail events like Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day, or specifically for students during Apple’s annual “Back to School” promotion. While Apple itself rarely offers direct price cuts on new hardware, third-party resellers frequently discount products throughout the year.

The optimal time to buy depends heavily on the product’s release cycle and the specific retailer, though:

iPhones: The best time to buy is often in the spring or summer, several months after the September launch, when third-party resellers begin offering deeper discounts . Conversely, the worst time is August, just before new models arrive and trigger price drops on older generations.

Macs and iPads: These see significant discounts during Black Friday (late November) and Amazon Prime Day (typically July and October). For students, the Back to School event (running June–September in the U.S. and July–October in the U.K.) is ideal, as Apple often bundles free accessories like AirPods or Apple Pencils with purchases.

Apple Watch: Major savings are typically found during Black Friday and Prime Day events.

2.

Are Apple refurbished deals worth it?

Apple refurbished deals are widely considered worth it, particularly when purchasing directly from the official Apple Refurbished Store, where products are restored to a “like-new” condition. While third-party resellers often provide steeper discounts, Apple’s own process is uniquely rigorous, offering a balance of significant savings and the same protections as a brand-new purchase.

Buying directly from Apple is often described as “almost indistinguishable” from buying new. According to our guide How much can you save at Apple’s Refurbished Store?, the company puts every device through a “stringent refurbishment process” that includes full functional testing, thorough cleaning, and inspection.

Key benefits of the official Apple Refurbished Store include:

Hardware Replacements: Refurbished iPads and iPhones receive a brand-new battery and outer shell .

Warranty and Support: All products come with a standard one-year limited warranty, 90 days of technical support, and are eligible for AppleCare .

Full Accessories: Devices are repackaged in a plain white box with all original manuals and cables .

Savings: You can typically save around 15% off the retail price for recent models, with much higher discounts on older generations.

Avoid the Apple price hikes: Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store sells products at the old, pre-hike prices – meaning you can effectively sidestep the recent price increases entirely.

3.

Is it better to buy Apple products from Amazon or Apple?

Deciding whether to buy Apple products from Amazon or directly from Apple depends on whether you prioritize immediate cost savings or the specific perks and guarantees offered by the manufacturer. While Amazon often provides deeper discounts, Apple offers unique benefits like trade-in credits, education pricing, and the assurance of receiving the latest models.

4.

Does Apple ever discount products directly?

Apple rarely provides direct price reductions on its new products, preferring to maintain steady Old MSRP pricing throughout a product’s lifecycle. Instead of traditional discounts, the company typically utilizes alternative methods to provide value directly to consumers, such as gift card incentives during major shopping events, education pricing, and a dedicated refurbished store.

While you will not often see a lower price tag on a new iPhone or Mac at the Apple Store, the company does offer several ways to save:

Apple Shopping Events: During events like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, Apple typically offers gift cards rather than price cuts. For example, in the 2025 holiday season, Apple provided gift cards ranging from $25 to $250 for eligible purchases.

Education Store: Students, teachers, and higher education staff can access year-round discounts on Macs and iPads . During the annual “Back to School” event, Apple often includes a “freebie” like AirPods or an Apple Pencil with qualifying purchases.

Apple Refurbished Store: This is the primary way to get a direct price reduction from Apple. Products are fully reconditioned, come with a one-year warranty, and can be discounted by hundreds of dollars or pounds.

Trade-In Program: Apple allows customers to trade in old devices to receive credit toward a new purchase, effectively lowering the out-of-pocket cost.

When are the best Apple deals?

Apple deals are generally best during major retail events like Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day, or specifically for students during Apple’s annual “Back to School” promotion. iPhones: The best time to buy is often in the spring or summer, several months after the September launch, when third-party resellers begin offering deeper discounts . Conversely, the worst time is August, just before new models arrive and trigger price drops on older generations.

Macs and iPads: These see significant discounts during Black Friday (late November) and Amazon Prime Day (typically July and October). For students, the Back to School event (running June–September in the U.S. and July–October in the U.K.) is ideal, as Apple often bundles free accessories like AirPods or Apple Pencils with purchases.

Buying directly from Apple is often described as “almost indistinguishable” from buying new. Avoid the Apple price hikes: Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store sells products at the old, pre-hike prices – meaning you can effectively sidestep the recent price increases entirely.

One of 2027's big-hitters.

New details regarding Kirby and the World Beyond have been revealed via Nintendo's winter catalogue in Japan (via Genki_JPN on X). While hardly comprehensive, it provides a little more insight into the game's story along with the abilities and environments available upon its release.

Of course, we know from the debut trailer that this will boast a much broader world than The Forgotten Land, with one detail noting how you can use Kirby's abilities to explore at your own pace. We also get a touch more context behind King Dedede's role, with the article stating that "a mysterious girl" has been kidnapped by the antagonist.
